questions.question: A ticket seller's maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) is 12 hours; recovery takes 6 hours to restore systems and 4 to check orders before selling. Which finding should the continuity planner record as MOST accurate?

options.A: The plan meets the MTD, with 2 hours to spare
options.B: The plan meets the MTD, with 6 hours to spare
options.C: The plan misses the MTD, as the RTO must equal it
options.D: The plan misses the MTD, as checks count toward the RPO

questions.key_concept: The full time until a function resumes, restoring systems plus checking work, must fit within the maximum tolerable downtime.
questions.pre_read: Add up every step between the outage and the first sale, then compare the total with the limit.
questions.correct_explanation: Selling resumes only after the systems are restored and the orders checked: 6 + 4 = 10 hours, inside the 12-hour MTD with 2 hours to spare. The 6-hour figure is the runner-up: it counts only the system restore, but customers cannot buy until the orders are checked, and that work time must also fit inside the MTD.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the systems are back in 6 hours. But selling waits for the 4 hours of checks too, so the function returns at 10 hours.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because both are time limits. But the RTO must fit inside the MTD, normally shorter, leaving room for work such as these checks.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because order checks involve data. But the RPO measures how much recent data can be lost; it says nothing about time to resume.

tips: Eliminate: C treats the RTO as equal to the MTD, though it must fit inside it, and D puts a time-to-resume task into the RPO.
Final two: A beats B because the function is down until the checks finish; restore time plus work time must fit inside the MTD.
Exam cue: add every step until the business function works again, then compare the total with the MTD. The RPO is about data lost, not time.

questions.question: A film studio runs a full backup each Sunday night and a differential backup every other night, and its file server fails on Thursday morning. Which backups are BEST for the IT technician to restore?

options.A: Sunday's full backup only
options.B: Sunday's full and the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday differentials
options.C: Wednesday's differential backup only
options.D: Sunday's full and Wednesday's differential

questions.key_concept: A differential backup holds all changes since the last full, so a restore needs the full plus only the latest differential.
questions.pre_read: Recall what each differential backup contains, counted from which earlier backup.
questions.correct_explanation: A differential backup holds every change since the last full backup, so Wednesday's differential already includes Monday's and Tuesday's changes. Restoring Sunday's full and then Wednesday's differential brings the server back to Wednesday night. Restoring all three differentials is the runner-up: that is the incremental rule, and here it repeats work the last differential already covers, which only lengthens the restore.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a full backup holds everything. But it holds everything as of Sunday; changes from Monday to Wednesday would be lost.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it would end in the same state. But each differential already holds every change since Sunday, so the earlier two only add restore time.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is the newest copy. But a differential holds only changes since the full backup; without Sunday's full, most files are missing.

tips: Eliminate: A stops at Sunday and loses three days of changes, and C has the changes but not the full backup they build on.
Final two: D beats B because each differential holds all changes since the full; restoring every night's set is the incremental rule.
Exam cue: a differential restore is the full plus the latest differential; an incremental restore is the full plus every incremental since, in order.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 5.1.2 (Maintenance of Data Security, Integrity, and Backup: full, incremental and differential backups); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.DS-11 (backups of data are created, protected, maintained and tested)

questions.question: A parts distributor's business impact analysis sets a one-day recovery time objective (RTO) for orders, and leaders want the cheapest site that meets it. Which site should the IT manager propose as BEST?

options.A: A hot site with live copies of current data
options.B: A cold site that has space, power and cooling only
options.C: A warm site with equipment ready and data to restore
options.D: A spare room in the head office with spare servers

questions.key_concept: Choose the least costly recovery site whose readiness still meets the RTO; readier sites cost more to keep.
questions.pre_read: Note the target recovery time and the cost limit, then check each site against both.
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery sites trade readiness for cost. A warm site has equipment and connections in place, so restoring data can bring orders back within about a day, at medium cost. A hot site is the runner-up: it would meet the target easily, but it costs the most to keep running, and leaders asked for the cheapest site that meets a one-day RTO.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a hot site meets a one-day target with room to spare. But it costs the most to keep ready, and leaders asked for the cheapest fit.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is the cheapest site. But equipping an empty room takes days to weeks, far beyond a one-day target.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it costs little and is close by. But a fire or flood at head office would take out the spare room too.

tips: Eliminate: B takes days or weeks to equip, missing the target, and D shares the main site, so one disaster hits both.
Final two: C beats A because both meet one day, but the warm site does it at lower cost; match the site to the RTO.
Exam cue: hot sites recover in hours or less, warm in about a day to a few days, cold in weeks. Pick the cheapest that still meets the RTO.

questions.question: At a marketing agency, senior managers skip the security awareness sessions every employee must attend, and staff attendance has fallen since. What should the awareness lead propose FIRST?

options.A: Ask senior managers to attend and speak at the sessions
options.B: Send staff firmer reminders that attendance is required
options.C: Tie each employee's yearly bonus to their attendance
options.D: Cancel the sessions, as falling attendance shows little interest

questions.key_concept: Leaders set security culture by example; when they skip required activities staff follow, so leadership participation comes first.
questions.pre_read: Notice who stopped attending first and what happened to everyone else afterward.
questions.correct_explanation: Staff copy what leaders do: when senior managers skip required sessions, everyone learns the rule is optional. The cause is the example at the top, so the first fix is leaders taking part visibly, attending and speaking. Firmer reminders to staff are the runner-up: they press on the symptom, while the managers' absence keeps teaching the opposite lesson.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: reminders do reinforce the rule. But they target staff while leaders keep skipping, so the message that sessions are optional continues.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because money motivates. But penalties build resentment, not culture, and they leave leaders still setting the opposite example.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because low attendance looks like low interest. But attendance fell after managers stopped going; the cause is their example, not the sessions.

tips: Eliminate: C leans on penalties, which build fear rather than security culture, and D drops required training because of a symptom.
Final two: A beats B because the cause is the leaders' example; reminders to staff treat the symptom while managers keep skipping.
Exam cue: security culture starts at the top. When leaders exempt themselves, fix their visible example before pressing everyone else.

questions.question: A city parking officer finds new quick response (QR) code stickers on pay machines that send drivers to a look-alike payment site. Which type of attack is this MOST accurately?

options.A: A smishing attack
options.B: A quishing attack
options.C: A vishing attack
options.D: A whaling attack

questions.key_concept: Phishing variants are named by channel or by target; a QR code that leads to a fake site is quishing.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the lure reaches its victims: by text, by call, by a scanned code or by targeting someone senior.
questions.correct_explanation: Quishing is phishing through a QR code: scanning it opens a fake site that collects payment or login details, and stickers placed over genuine codes are a common method. Smishing is the runner-up: victims also land on a fake site on their phone, but smishing arrives by text message, and here the lure is a printed code on the machine.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the fake site opens on a phone. But smishing arrives as a text message; this lure is a printed code that drivers scan.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is another phone-based scam. But vishing uses voice calls, and no one here is called.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is a named variant. But whaling targets senior executives; these stickers target any driver who parks.

tips: Eliminate: C needs a voice call, and D targets executives; neither fits a printed code aimed at any driver.
Final two: B beats A because the lure arrives through a scanned code, not a text message; smishing is named for SMS.
Exam cue: most phishing variants are named by channel: smishing by text, vishing by voice, quishing by QR code. Whaling and spear phishing are named by target.

questions.question: At a design agency's badge-controlled door, someone in a courier uniform carrying boxes asks an employee to hold it open. What is the employee's BEST response?

options.A: Hold the door and help carry the boxes inside
options.B: Check the courier's ID card, then hold the door
options.C: Let them in, then report it if they act oddly
options.D: Direct them to reception to sign in and be collected

questions.key_concept: Never let unbadged people through a controlled door; send them to reception, because uniforms and ID cards are easy to fake.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the person is asking for, and what the badge reader on the door is meant to check.
questions.correct_explanation: Holding a controlled door for someone without a badge is piggybacking, and a courier uniform with boxes is a classic way to get it. The safe, polite answer is to send them to reception, where visits are checked and staff come to collect them. Checking their ID card is the runner-up: it feels like verification, but the card comes from the visitor and is easy to fake.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because helping is polite. But holding a controlled door lets an unverified person past the badge reader, which is what the story aims for.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: checking ID feels careful. But the visitor supplies the card and it is easy to fake; verification needs a channel the organization controls.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because reporting is good practice. But once inside, an intruder can act at once; the badge reader exists to stop entry, not record it.

tips: Eliminate: A lets an unverified person past the badge reader, and C reports only after access is already given.
Final two: D beats B because verification must come through a channel you trust; an ID card the visitor carries proves little.
Exam cue: uniforms, boxes and urgency are props. Send anyone without a badge to the proper check-in point instead of judging them yourself.

questions.question: A regional broadcaster's awareness course still teaches staff to spot phishing by spelling mistakes, though attackers now use AI to write fluent lures. Which change should the awareness lead make FIRST?

options.A: Teach staff to recognize the writing style of AI tools
options.B: Install an AI-text detector on email and retire the old course
options.C: Teach staff to verify unusual requests through known channels
options.D: Run the existing course twice a year instead of once

questions.key_concept: AI makes phishing fluent, so awareness training should teach verifying requests through known channels, not judging spelling or style.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the course teaches staff to look for, and what attackers can now do about it.
questions.correct_explanation: AI tools now write fluent, personal messages, so polish no longer separates real from fake. Training should shift from how a message looks to what it asks: an unusual payment, password or urgent request gets checked through a channel the staff member already trusts. Teaching AI writing style is the runner-up: it still judges polish, and AI text is too varied to spot reliably.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: real AI examples belong in training. But spotting AI style is unreliable; staff need a habit that works however polished the message is.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a tool scales. But AI-text detectors miss much and flag genuine mail; no filter replaces people who verify odd requests.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because repetition builds habits. But repeating outdated advice twice as often teaches the wrong habit twice as well.

tips: Eliminate: B hands judgment to an unreliable detector and drops training, and D repeats outdated content more often.
Final two: C beats A because verification works on any lure; judging writing style fails once AI makes lures fluent.
Exam cue: against AI-written lures and deepfakes, teach process, not polish. Check the request through a known channel before acting.

questions.question: A shop assistant must set a new password for the store's ordering system, which accepts up to 64 characters. Which choice BEST follows current password advice?

options.A: Four random words joined into one long passphrase
options.B: Eight characters mixing symbols, numbers and capital letters
options.C: The old password with its final number raised by one
options.D: A favorite team's name with the current year added

questions.key_concept: Length beats complexity: a long passphrase of random words is stronger and easier to remember than a short complex password.
questions.pre_read: Notice the length the system allows, and compare how hard each choice would be to guess.
questions.correct_explanation: Length does most of the work: four random words make a long passphrase that is hard to guess and easy to remember, and current guidance favors length over forced complexity. The eight-character mixed password is the runner-up: symbols look strong, but short passwords fall quickly to guessing tools, and people tend to use predictable patterns, such as a capital first and a number last.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: mixed characters feel strong. But eight characters is short, people follow predictable patterns, and length adds far more strength.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is easy to remember. But attackers who know an old password try small changes like this first.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is personal. But team names and years are common, and easy to find on social media.

tips: Eliminate: C changes one predictable character of a known password, and D uses public, common details attackers try early.
Final two: A beats B because length beats complexity; a long passphrase resists guessing far better than eight mixed characters.
Exam cue: when a system allows long passwords, choose length, such as several random words. Keep each one unique, in a password manager.

questions.question: During a restructuring at a car manufacturer, the awareness lead drafts a phishing simulation announcing surprise job cuts, expecting high engagement. Which change to the plan is BEST?

options.A: Send the job-cut lure only to staff who clicked before
options.B: Announce the test date so staff know to watch for it
options.C: Keep the job-cut lure, since realistic tests teach the most
options.D: Use a realistic lure that causes no real distress instead

questions.key_concept: Phishing simulations should be realistic but must avoid lures that cause real distress, since trust drives reporting.
questions.pre_read: Notice what is happening to staff right now, and how this lure would land on them.
questions.correct_explanation: Simulations exist to build skills and trust. A lure about job cuts during a real restructuring causes genuine fear and anger that outlast the test and damage reporting, while a realistic lure without that harm still teaches staff to spot phishing. Keeping the job-cut lure is the runner-up: realism matters, but realism bought with real distress costs more trust than it teaches.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because past clickers need practice. But aiming a distressing lure at them feels punitive and makes them less likely to report.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because warning staff seems fair. But staff then watch only on that day; saying that tests happen at random is enough.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: realistic lures do teach well. But this one exploits a real fear during real job changes, damaging trust in the security team.

tips: Eliminate: A singles out past clickers, which reads as punishment, and B announces the date, which turns the test into a memory exercise.
Final two: D beats C because simulations must teach without real harm; a job-cut lure during restructuring costs the trust reporting depends on.
Exam cue: good simulations are realistic, approved in advance, no-blame and never cruel. Trust is what makes people report real attacks.

questions.question: A software reseller's phishing report rate jumped from 20% to 55% once reports from a new email button were counted with help desk calls. What should the reporting analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Present the rise as proof that awareness training is working
options.B: Note the counting change and mark where the trend restarts
options.C: Report the new figure as usual, as the data is more complete
options.D: Drop the metric, since its figures can no longer be trusted

questions.key_concept: Metrics must be collected the same way each period; when the method changes, record it and restart the baseline.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed at the same moment the number jumped.
questions.correct_explanation: A metric is comparable over time only if it is measured the same way. Counting button reports as well as calls changed the method, so much of the jump may reflect the new count, not new behavior. The analyst notes the change and marks the break. Reporting the new figure as usual is the runner-up: the data is better, but a silent method change makes the jump look like progress.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the number moved the right way. But the counting changed at the same time, so the rise cannot be credited to training.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the new data is more complete. But changing the method without a note makes old and new figures look comparable when they are not.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the trend broke. But the metric is still useful; noting the change and building a new baseline keeps it meaningful.

tips: Eliminate: A credits training with a rise the new counting may explain, and D drops a useful metric instead of noting the method change.
Final two: B beats C because a quiet method change breaks the trend; better data still needs a note so readers compare like with like.
Exam cue: when the way a number is counted changes, record the change and restart the baseline. Comparable beats impressive.

questions.subtopic: 2.4 Measuring effectiveness. Using measurement to improve
questions.question: A cruise line's server team took 40 days on average to apply critical patches, against a 14-day target, so the IT manager added a weekly patch window. What is the metrics analyst's BEST next step?

options.A: Mark the patching gap closed now the window is in place
options.B: Raise the target to 40 days to match current results
options.C: Track patch times over the coming months against the target
options.D: Add three new patch metrics to the monthly dashboard

questions.key_concept: After a fix, measure again against the target before closing the issue; a process change is not proof of a better outcome.
questions.pre_read: Notice what has changed so far: the process, or the result.
questions.correct_explanation: A fix is an expectation until the numbers confirm it. The analyst keeps measuring patch times against the 14-day target over the next few months to see whether the weekly window closes the gap, and reports the result to the IT manager. Marking the gap closed is the runner-up: the fix is in place, but a change in process is not yet a change in outcome.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a fix has been made. But nobody yet knows whether patches now land within 14 days; closing the gap before measuring assumes success.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the metric would turn green. But moving the target to match poor results hides the risk instead of reducing it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because more data seems helpful. But the existing metric already answers the question; more charts do not show whether the fix worked.

tips: Eliminate: B moves the target to fit the problem, and D adds metrics when the existing one already answers the question.
Final two: C beats A because only a new measurement shows whether the fix worked; a process change is not yet a better outcome.
Exam cue: improvement is a loop. Find the cause, fix it with an owner, then measure again before calling it done.

questions.question: A rail operator's IT team tracks the share of new starters with working accounts on day one, against a 95% service target. What is this metric MOST accurately?

options.A: A key risk indicator warning of rising exposure
options.B: A risk appetite statement set by the board
options.C: A risk tolerance limit for a single named risk
options.D: A key performance indicator tracking a goal

questions.key_concept: A KPI measures a process against its goal; a KRI warns that a named risk is growing toward its tolerance.
questions.pre_read: Ask what this figure is compared with, and what anyone would do if it dropped.
questions.correct_explanation: A key performance indicator shows how well a process meets its goal, and this one compares day-one accounts with a 95% service target. If it falls, the fix is to improve onboarding. The key risk indicator is the runner-up: the same kind of number can be a KRI, but only when it warns that a named risk is growing toward its limit, and this one judges service delivery.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: KPIs and KRIs can look alike. But this figure is judged against a service target, which makes it a measure of performance, not an early warning.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it involves a target. But an appetite statement is the board's broad view of how much risk to take, not a measured result.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because 95% sounds like a limit. But a tolerance bounds a risk; this number measures how well a service is delivered.

tips: Eliminate: B and C are risk limits that leaders set, not measured results, so neither describes a figure tracked against a target.
Final two: D beats A because the figure judges a process against its goal; a KRI warns that a named risk is getting worse.
Exam cue: ask what the number is judged against. A goal or service target makes it a KPI; a risk and its tolerance make it a KRI.

questions.question: After a competitor's breach, a retailer's board lowers its tolerance for unpatched payment systems, and the risk owner approves key risk indicator (KRI) thresholds. What should the dashboard analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the risk owner to approve thresholds matching the new tolerance
options.B: Tell the risk owner the current thresholds still fit
options.C: Tighten the dashboard's thresholds to match the board's new tolerance
options.D: Add a KRI that tracks news of the competitor's breach

questions.key_concept: KRI thresholds are set from risk tolerance; when tolerance changes, the thresholds are revised and approved by the risk owner.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the board changed and who approves the numbers on the dashboard.
questions.correct_explanation: Thresholds are where a tolerance meets the dashboard: when leaders change the tolerance, the thresholds must change with it, or the colors keep judging the old limit. The risk owner approves thresholds, so the analyst proposes new ones for approval. Tightening them directly is the runner-up: the numbers may be right, but changing approved limits alone bypasses the owner's decision.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because nothing has turned red. But the colors are judged against the old tolerance; under the new one, today's green may already be too much risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the thresholds do need tightening. But the risk owner approves them; an analyst changing limits alone bypasses that decision.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the breach prompted the change. But news about another firm is not a measure of this retailer's own unpatched systems.

tips: Eliminate: B judges risk against a tolerance leaders have replaced, and D tracks news about another firm instead of the retailer's own exposure.
Final two: A beats C because the risk owner approves thresholds; the analyst proposes the change rather than making it alone.
Exam cue: thresholds come from tolerance. When the tolerance, the business or the threats change, revisit the thresholds with whoever owns them.

questions.question: A patent firm's AI policy allows two approved assistants, and its security team wants a key risk indicator (KRI) for client data leaking through other AI tools. Which measure BEST fits?

options.A: Staff completion rate for the AI policy course
options.B: Weekly visits from firm devices to unapproved AI services
options.C: Number of licenses bought for the approved assistants
options.D: Number of help desk tickets about approved assistants

questions.key_concept: An AI risk indicator should track the risky behavior itself, such as use of unapproved AI tools, not training completion.
questions.pre_read: Name the risk in the stem, then ask which number would rise before that risk turns into harm.
questions.correct_explanation: A KRI should warn early that a named risk is growing. Visits to unapproved AI services measure the very behavior that leaks client data, and a rising count signals trouble before a breach. Course completion is the runner-up: training supports the policy, but completion shows who sat the course, not whether anyone is pasting client files into other tools.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: training supports the AI policy. But completion is an implementation measure; it shows who finished a course, not whether staff use unapproved tools.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because licenses show adoption. But buying licenses for approved tools says nothing about use of the unapproved ones that leak data.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tickets show how staff use AI. But support requests about approved tools measure their usability, not leakage elsewhere.

tips: Eliminate: C and D measure the approved assistants, while the risk sits in tools outside the approved list.
Final two: B beats A because a KRI tracks the risky behavior itself; course completion shows training happened, not that behavior changed.
Exam cue: a good AI KRI measures the behavior or condition that creates the risk, such as unapproved tool use, drift or rising overrides.
